title: Money: Earning, Owing and Giving
question: Why is the longest verse in the Quran about a debt?
intro: The Quran does not treat wealth as dirty. Trade is lawful, honest earning is honourable, and the Prophet ﷺ himself traded as a merchant before his mission. But money is also where people are most tempted to take what is not theirs.

So the Quran guards every step: how wealth is earned (no riba, no cheating, no bribery), how it is recorded (debts written and witnessed), and how it is used (no hoarding, no waste, and a share for others). Wealth is held in trust: Allah made us successors over it (57:7).
Riba, often translated as usury or interest, was forbidden in stages. Today you will trace those stages and see why the Quran insists that trade and riba are not the same thing.

passages.context: Madinah. Ibn 'Abbas is reported in al-Bukhari as saying the verse on riba was the last revealed.
passages.point: Believers must drop any interest still owed to them and keep only their principal: no one wrongs and no one is wronged. 2:275 adds that Allah permitted trade and forbade riba.
passages.label: stated

passages.from: O you who have believed, when you contract a debt
passages.context: The longest verse in the Quran, placed right after the verses on riba.
passages.point: Write down every debt with a term, small or large, through a fair scribe and with witnesses. The verse says this is more just and prevents doubt between people.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: Opens al-Mutaffifin, "those who give short measure", a surah named after cheating in the market.
passages.point: Woe to those who demand full measure for themselves but short-change others. 83:4-6 reminds them that they will stand before the Lord of the worlds.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: Part of the moral code of al-Isra, revealed in Makkah.
passages.point: Give relatives, the poor and travellers their right, and do not waste. If you cannot give, speak gently. Keep the balance: no hand chained to the neck, nor stretched out until nothing is left.
passages.label: stated

visual.title: Riba, step by step
visual.caption: A common scholarly reading of the riba verses as a gradual path, like the stages on alcohol. The dating of the middle steps is approximate.
visual.label: explained

items.label: Not with Allah
items.text: Makkah: interest does not grow with Allah; zakah multiplies.

items.label: A past people's wrong
items.text: Some of the Children of Israel took it though it was forbidden.

items.label: Doubled and multiplied
items.text: First direct ban for believers. Most scholars: "doubled" describes, not limits.

items.label: The final ban
items.text: Trade allowed, riba forbidden; keep your principal, wrong no one.

items.label: Ease for debtors
items.text: Give a struggling debtor time; forgiving the debt is better.

word.nuance: Literally growth, from the same root as rabwah, a hill that rises (23:50). In law it is a gain stipulated on a loan and, from hadith, certain unequal swaps of like goods. The Quran turns the word around: Allah destroys riba and makes charity grow (yurbī, 2:276).

mixup.myth: Islam disapproves of wealth and of making money.
mixup.truth: Trade by mutual consent is lawful (4:29), and the Prophet ﷺ was a trader before his mission. What the Quran forbids is unjust gain: riba, bribery (2:188), cheating, and hoarding that withholds what is due (9:34). It praises those who spend by night and day (2:274) and calls our wealth something we hold as successors (57:7).

remember: Trade is lawful and riba is not; the Quran rejects the claim that they are alike (2:275).
Write down debts, give full measure, and give a struggling debtor time (2:282, 83:1-3, 2:280).
Spend with balance, neither stingy nor wasteful, and give others their right (17:26-29, 25:67).

quiz.q: What is the longest verse in the Quran about?
quiz.why: 2:282, the longest verse, sets out how to record a debt with a scribe and witnesses, "whether it is small or large".

quiz.q: When a believer gives up riba, what may they keep (2:279)?
quiz.why: 2:279: "if you repent, you may have your principal - [thus] you do no wrong, nor are you wronged."

quiz.q: What does 2:280 say to do when a debtor is in hardship?
quiz.why: 2:280: "[let there be] postponement until [a time of] ease. But if you give [from your right as] charity, then it is better for you."

reflect: Where in your spending this week could you move a little closer to the balance of 25:67?
